title: The Ephesus riot (Acts 19:21–41)
hook: silversmiths start a riot for Artemis; a town clerk calms the crowd
tomorrow: a sermon runs past midnight. a young man is sitting in the window…

segments.voice: In Ephesus the books burned, and the word grew. Then the city's silversmiths do some counting of their own, and they don't like the numbers.

A comment thread can go from zero to furious in one afternoon, and half the people in it couldn't tell you how it started. Ephesus, a packed theater: "Great is Diana of the Ephesians." The crowd shouts it again and again, Acts says "about the space of two hours." Two of Paul's companions, Gaius and Aristarchus, have been dragged in. Paul wants to go in after them; his friends won't let him. Then one man walks out in front of the crowd. Not an apostle. The town clerk.
screen: `ZERO TO FURIOUS.` → `GREAT IS DIANA, FOR TWO HOURS.` → `ENTER THE TOWN CLERK.`

segments.voice: Rewind to how it started. Demetrius, a silversmith who makes silver shrines of the goddess, calls the craftsmen together: "Sirs, ye know that by this craft we have our wealth." Paul has been saying that gods made with hands are no gods, so their trade is in danger, and so is the goddess's honor. The King James calls her Diana; the Greek names her Artemis. Tempers catch, and "the whole city was filled with confusion." Inside the theater, Acts gives a detail that's almost funny: "Some therefore cried one thing, and some another: for the assembly was confused; and the more part knew not wherefore they were come together." Most of the crowd doesn't know why it's there. Now the town clerk. He quiets them, and makes a plain case. Everyone knows this city honors its goddess. These men are "neither robbers of churches, nor yet blasphemers of your goddess." If Demetrius has a complaint, the courts are open. "Ye ought to be quiet, and to do nothing rashly." Then "he dismissed the assembly." Here's the one to tell a friend tonight: the peacemaker in this chapter isn't one of Paul's people at all. Acts lets a city official, loyal to his own city's goddess, be the calm voice in the room, and tells it with respect.
screen: `BY THIS CRAFT WE HAVE OUR WEALTH.` · `THEY KNEW NOT WHY THEY CAME.` · `THE COURTS ARE OPEN.` · `A PEACEMAKER FROM OUTSIDE.` · then, large: `BE QUIET, DO NOTHING RASHLY.`

segments.voice: Sit or stand tall, and rest your hands open, palms down, the way someone signals a room to settle. Let your breathing slow until it's slower than a shout. Stay there, and let one heated conversation from this week come to mind without joining it. A room gets calmer when even one person stops adding to the noise.
The Ephesus riot. Two hours of shouting in a theater, and a town clerk who quieted it.
Your line: be quiet, do nothing rashly. A town clerk said it, and a whole theater went home. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1520 COUNTS.` → `ACTS, READ THROUGH · 34 OF 45.` → `TOMORROW: A SERMON RUNS PAST MIDNIGHT. A YOUNG MAN IS SITTING IN THE WINDOW…`

howItsDone: Christians read the Ephesus riot in Acts 19 in church and Bible study; some teachers point to the town clerk when talking about keeping calm in conflict.

fork.setup: two dads start yelling in the stands at your little brother's basketball game, and people pull out phones. you're closest. what would the town clerk do?
options: lower the temperature, then point them to the ref and the rules.
work out which dad is right and back him up, loudly.
film it too, so there's a record of who started it.
fork.reveal: the clerk quieted the crowd, said do nothing rashly, and sent the complaint to the courts. calm first, then the proper place.

original.note: Greek: assembly. Acts 19:32 and 19:41 use it for the crowd in the theater.

trapdoor: what you thought: the town clerk took Paul's side.
what it means: he took no side; he told the crowd to be quiet, do nothing rashly, and use the courts.
what a scholar hears: the Greek calls that confused crowd an ekklesia, an assembly, the same word Acts uses for the church.
guess: a theater crowd shouting for hours over a trade
a revolt of Roman soldiers against Paul
a fire that destroyed a temple in Ephesus

chat.meaning: The town clerk quieted the crowd, said do nothing rashly, and pointed them to the courts: calm first, then the proper place to settle it.

Artemis.meaning: a Greek goddess honored in Ephesus

Demetrius.meaning: a silversmith in Ephesus who made shrines of the goddess

town clerk.meaning: a city official who spoke for public order

notes: The KJV names the goddess Diana; the Greek text of Acts 19 has Artemis (the index hook says Artemis). Confirm the line 'the Greek names her Artemis'.

The trapdoor says the Greek word for the theater crowd (Acts 19:32, 41) is ekklesia, the word Acts also uses for the church. Confirm with a scholar; cut it if it breaks the claims rule. It is no longer in the spoken text.

Unity thread (light touch): 'the peacemaker in this chapter isn't one of Paul's people… a city official, loyal to his own city's goddess' reads Acts 19:35–41, where the clerk speaks of the city as keeper of the goddess's temple. 'Tells it with respect' is a reading of the passage's tone. Confirm both.
'The whole city was filled with confusion' is quoted from 19:29 with a lowercase start inside the sentence; KJV reads 'And the whole city…'.
